text: Writing a design document that actually gets approved. An ADR documents a decision after it's made. A design document is the artifact that gets a significant decision made in the first place -- circulated before building starts, read by the people whose buy-in actually matters, and either approved, sent back for revision, or rejected.

This lesson covers the structure and the specific habits that separate a design doc that gets a clear, timely decision from one that stalls in review for weeks with no one quite willing to say yes or no.

A design doc that drives a decision has five sections, in order. Problem states the gap it needs to close. Goals and Non-Goals names what the design will, and deliberately will not, attempt to solve -- because the fastest way for a review to stall is reviewers debating a problem the document never claimed to address. Proposed Design is the actual architecture. Alternatives Considered names the real options and why they were rejected. And Risks plus a phased Rollout Plan closes it out.

Here's the single most common reason design docs stall. A document that presents only one option, with no visible alternatives, forces reviewers into an all-or-nothing choice -- approve this exact plan, or reject it and start over. A reviewer with a real but partial objection, 'I like this but worry about X,' has nowhere to put that feedback except a full rejection, so the document just sits in limbo. Real alternatives give that reviewer a path to say 'I prefer this, but let's address one risk' -- a decision, not a stall.

Every reviewer is implicitly checking for three objections. What does this cost, and who's actually paying for it? What happens when this breaks -- does the Risks section honestly name real risks, not a token 'risks: none'? And what did you not consider, and why -- which Alternatives Considered answers before anyone has to ask it out loud. Pre-empting these three in the document itself turns the review meeting into confirming a decision the doc already made the case for.

And length is usually a symptom, not a virtue. A fifteen-page design doc is rarely more thorough than a three-page one -- it's usually a sign the author hasn't yet figured out what the actual decision is, and is describing everything they know instead of making the specific case for one proposal.

Get the structure right, name the non-goals, show real alternatives, and a design doc drives a decision instead of stalling in review.
